# Conjecture 2.81

by L. N. Shevrin

Does there exist an axiomatizable class of lattices such that the lattice of
all subsemigroups of a semigroup belongs to that class up to isomorphism if
and only if the semigroup is a free group? The same question is asked for
free abelian groups.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«2.81»

universe u

/-- The two binary function symbols in the first-order language of lattices. -/
inductive LatticeFunction : ℕ → Type
  | sup : LatticeFunction 2
  | inf : LatticeFunction 2

/-- The first-order language of lattices, with binary join and meet. -/
def latticeLanguage : FirstOrder.Language where
  Functions := LatticeFunction
  Relations := fun _ ↦ Empty

/-- The interpretation of the first-order lattice language on a lattice. -/
def latticeStructure (L : Type*) [Lattice L] : latticeLanguage.Structure L where
  funMap := fun {n} f ↦ match n, f with
    | _, .sup => fun x ↦ x 0 ⊔ x 1
    | _, .inf => fun x ↦ x 0 ⊓ x 1
  RelMap := fun {_} r ↦ nomatch r

namespace parts

/--
Does there exist a class $\mathfrak K$ of lattices, axiomatized by an arbitrary
set of first-order sentences in the language with meet and join, such that,
for every semigroup $S$, the lattice of all subsemigroups of $S$ is isomorphic
to a member of $\mathfrak K$ if and only if $S$ is the multiplicative
semigroup of a free group of arbitrary rank? Here `Subsemigroup S` includes
the empty subsemigroup, and rank zero (the trivial group) is allowed.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 6 20]
theorem a : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ T : latticeLanguage.Theory,
      ∀ (S : Type u) [Semigroup S] [Nonempty S],
        (∃ (L : Type u) (_ : Lattice L),
          @FirstOrder.Language.Theory.Model latticeLanguage L (latticeStructure L) T ∧
            Nonempty (Subsemigroup S ≃o L)) ↔
          ∃ X : Type u, Nonempty (S ≃* FreeGroup X) := by
  sorry

/--
Does there exist a class $\mathfrak K$ of lattices, axiomatized by an arbitrary
set of first-order sentences in the language with meet and join, such that,
for every semigroup $S$, the lattice of all subsemigroups of $S$ is isomorphic
to a member of $\mathfrak K$ if and only if $S$ is the multiplicative
semigroup of a free abelian group of arbitrary rank? Here `Subsemigroup S`
includes the empty subsemigroup, and rank zero (the trivial group) is allowed.
-/

theorem b : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ T : latticeLanguage.Theory,
      ∀ (S : Type u) [Semigroup S] [Nonempty S],
        (∃ (L : Type u) (_ : Lattice L),
          @FirstOrder.Language.Theory.Model latticeLanguage L (latticeStructure L) T ∧
            Nonempty (Subsemigroup S ≃o L)) ↔
          ∃ X : Type u, Nonempty (S ≃* Multiplicative (FreeAbelianGroup X)) := by
  sorry

by L. N. Shevrin

a) Does there exist an axiomatizable class of lattices $\mathfrak{K}$ such that the
lattice of all subsemigroups of a semigroup $S$ is isomorphic to some lattice in
$\mathfrak{K}$ if and only if $S$ is a free group?

b) The same question for free abelian groups.

Analogous questions have affirmative answers for torsion-free groups, for non-periodic
groups, for abelian torsion-free groups, for abelian non-periodic groups, for orderable
groups (the corresponding classes of lattices are even finitely axiomatizable). Thus, in
the posed questions one may assume from the outset that the semigroup $S$ is a
torsion-free group (respectively, a torsion-free abelian group).

## Formalisation notes

An *axiomatizable class of lattices* is the class of all lattices satisfying a set $T$ of
first-order sentences. We take $T$ to be a theory in the first-order language
`Language.order` with a single binary relation symbol $\leq$, interpreted in a lattice $L$
as the lattice order (`Language.order.OrderedStructure L`). Since the lattice operations
$\wedge, \vee$ and the lattice order $\leq$ are first-order definable from each other, a
class of lattices is axiomatizable in the language $\{\leq\}$ if and only if it is
axiomatizable in the language $\{\wedge, \vee\}$, so this is no loss of generality.

The lattice of all subsemigroups of $S$ is `Subsemigroup S`; it contains the empty
subsemigroup as its least element. A lattice isomorphism is an order isomorphism `≃o`.

A semigroup $S$ "is a free group" when it is isomorphic, as a semigroup, to a free group
`FreeGroup α` on some set `α` (of any cardinality, including the empty set); likewise
for free abelian groups, using `Multiplicative (FreeAbelianGroup α)`.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)

/-!
# Conjecture 2.81

by L. N. Shevrin

a) Does there exist an axiomatizable class of lattices $\mathfrak{K}$ such that the
lattice of all subsemigroups of a semigroup $S$ is isomorphic to some lattice in
$\mathfrak{K}$ if and only if $S$ is a free group?

b) The same question for free abelian groups.

The notebook remarks that the analogous questions have affirmative answers for
torsion-free groups, non-periodic groups, abelian torsion-free groups, abelian
non-periodic groups and orderable groups (with finitely axiomatizable classes of
lattices), so that one may assume from the outset that $S$ is a torsion-free group
(respectively, a torsion-free abelian group). We formalize the questions as posed,
i.e. for all semigroups $S$.

## Formalization notes

* The lattice of all subsemigroups of $S$ is `Subsemigroup S`; following the standard
  convention, the empty subsemigroup `⊥` is included (without it the subsemigroups of
  $S$ need not form a lattice).
* An *axiomatizable* class of lattices is an elementary class: the class of all
  lattices satisfying some set $T$ of first-order sentences. We use Mathlib's
  language `FirstOrder.Language.order`, whose only symbol is a binary relation
  interpreted as `≤`; since `≤` and the lattice operations are first-order
  definable from one another, the axiomatizable classes of lattices are the same
  in the signature $\{\le\}$ and in the signature $\{\vee, \wedge\}$.
* "The semigroup $S$ is a free group" means that $S$ is isomorphic, as a
  semigroup, to `FreeGroup X` for some set `X` (of any cardinality, including the
  empty set, so that the trivial group counts as free). Similarly, "$S$ is a free
  abelian group" means that $S$ is isomorphic to the (multiplicatively written)
  free abelian group `FreeAbelianGroup X` on some set `X`.
